Why go: Thailand's national sport, live

Muay Thai is a ritual as well as a fight. Before each bout, fighters perform the wai kru, a slow dance that honours their teachers, while a small band plays a pipe-and-drum tune that speeds up through the rounds. A card in Chaweng typically mixes young local fighters, experienced Thai professionals and foreign fighters training on the island, ending with the night's main event. Rounds are 3 minutes, and the crowd gets loud when the clinch work starts.

Two stadiums in Chaweng share the week. Phetchbuncha fights on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday and is the more traditional, local-feeling venue. Samui International fights on Tuesday, Friday and Sunday, with a bigger production and more seat levels up to a VIP lounge. Check your night first, then choose the stadium.

Who it suits, and who should choose something else

  • Good for: first-time visitors curious about Thai culture, sports fans, and groups who want a night out in Chaweng that isn't just bars.
  • Choose something else if: combat sports upset you. Fighters get hurt, and some on the early cards are teenagers. If you'd rather train than watch, see our Muay Thai gyms and classes guide.
  • Families: children are allowed, but fights finish around midnight and it is loud. Phetchbuncha is cheaper for kids.

Good to know

  • Getting there: both stadiums are in Chaweng, a short walk from central Chaweng hotels. Agree the taxi fare before you get in.
  • Holidays: on Buddhist holy days, when alcohol sales are banned, cards can move or change. We'll tell you if your night is affected.
  • Betting: you'll see locals betting with hand signals. Stay out of it as a visitor.
